newsitem.title: USA: Film stars send letter of protest to China.
newsitem.headline: Film stars send letter of protest to China.

text.p: A group of movie luminaries including Paul Newman and Bernardo Bertolucci wrote to China's ambassador to the United States on Wednesday protesting Beijing's "attempt to impose worldwide censorship" on films in or about China.

The letter, sent under the auspices of the New York-based non-governmental Human Rights Watch, was written mainly in response to Beijing warning the Walt Disney Company last month that its ambitious business plans in China were at risk if it went ahead with the release of a movie on the Dalai Lama, Tibet's exiled religious leader.

"We are urging Disney, other film companies, and all of those involved in the industry including actors, producers and directors to actively and publicly oppose any and all attempts by your government to censor or intimidate them," said the letter to Ambassador Li Daoyu, which included the names of 41 directors, producers, actors and actresses.

The Burbank, California-based entertainment giant has already responded publicly over the production of "Kundun", a film about the early life of the Dalai Lama, who fled to India with many of his followers in 1959 after years of resisting China's control of the Himalayan region.
Human rights advocates have for years condemned the communist government's policy toward Tibet as repressive.
Disney said in a terse statement on Nov. 26 that it would go ahead with the domestic release of the film, made by renowned director Martin Scorsese.
"Kundun", which means "The Presence", is being co-produced by Disney's Touchstone Pictures and Refuge Productions and being shot in Morocco. It was expected to be released in late 1997.
Disney declined comment on the Human Rights Watch correspondence with the Chinese diplomat.

China has not objected to another movie about the Dalai Lama called "Seven Years in Tibet" starring Brad Pitt. It is being filmed in Argentina, Chile and Canada by Sony's Tri-Star division and tells the story of an Austrian mountain climber who befriended the young Dalai Lama after the Second World War.

The letter alleged that China's warning to Disney was the latest incident in a persistent effort by the Beijing government to censor the film industry. They included a list of 12 occasions when they believed the government had interfered with productions.

"The interference that concerns us is your government's attempt to impose worldwide censorship on any artistic production that does not meet with government approval," said the group, which also included Susan Sarandon, Nora Ephron, Spike Lee, Tim Robbins, Barbra Streisand and Richard Gere, an actor who has long supported the Tibetan spiritual movement.
"We are eager for good relations with your government and with our Chinese colleagues, but respect for freedom of expression must underpin those ties," the letter said.
